Machine Learning on Graphs (UE23CS343BB4) is a Elective-4 offered in Semester 6. Credits: L=4 T=0 P=0 S=4 Total=4. Tools/Languages used: NetworkX for statistical features of. About this course: This course introduces the students to the three meta landscapes of representation, optimization, and objective for the learning tasks on graph data. Graphs are ubiquitous in almost everything today –in social graphs, large-scale biological systems, road networks, polypharmacy, and user-item relations. Graphs, being non-Euclidean, require different machine-learning approaches. This course starts by exploring graph features for traditional machine learning on graphs and discussing a few noteworthy classical graph ML approaches. The second unit focuses on shallow embedding methods for graphs in general, and then the same for knowledge graphs. The third unit focuses on representation learning using graph neural networks and discusses key algorithms along with extensions like temporal graphs and multi-relational graphs. The fourth unit discusses the deep generative models on the graph and model- building techniques using graph neural networks. The theory input concludes with a discussion on the interdisciplinary applications of Graph Neural Networks, interpretability, and meta-learning perspectives of graph AI.

text: Video Processing and understanding — Unit 2: Video segmentation, motion estimation, and tracking (14 hours). Topics covered: Video segmentation: Scene cut detection, spatio-temporal segmentation, Motion Detection and estimation (frame differencing, background subtraction, optical flow methods: Lucas-Kanade, Horn-Schunck), Spatial Feature extraction: 2D CNN, Skeletal keypoint detection, Temporal feature extraction: 3D CNN, temporal pooling, Object tracking: Kalman filter, DeepSORT.

text: After completing Automotive Cybersecurity (UE23CS342BB11), students will be able to: 1. Understand the fundamental principles of automotive cybersecurity, including key vehicle communication protocols and typical attack surfaces in modern vehicles. 2. Analyze and model threats and risks in automotive systems using structured methodologies such as TARA, STRIDE, and MITRE ATT&CK. 3. Apply secure design principles, cryptographic techniques, and secure coding practices to develop resilient automotive software and communication systems. 4. Evaluate and simulate real-world attack scenarios on automotive networks using industry tools (e.g., CANoe, Wireshark, VehicleSpy, Python) to test intrusion detection and mitigation strategies. 5. Interpret and implement cybersecurity standards and regulations such as ISO/SAE 21434 and UNECE WP.29 across the vehicle development lifecycle.

The objectives of Automotive Cybersecurity (UE23CS342BB11) are: 1. Focus on Threats and Defense: To provide students with the core knowledge to identify, analyze, and mitigate cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities in modern connected and autonomous vehicles, and to understand industry standards and best practices for vehicle protection. 2. Focus on Cybersecurity Landscape: To develop students' understanding of the automotive cybersecurity landscape, including key threats, defensive strategies, and relevant industry standards for securing vehicle electronics and communication networks. 3. Emphasizing Practical Skills: To provide students with essential knowledge of automotive systems, attack vectors, and security mechanisms, enabling them to contribute to the development and implementation of cybersecurity measures in the automotive industry.
